```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```


The traditional use-case of a phenology model is to predict a certain phenological stage,
for example full bloom, which defined accoridng to the BBCH scale as the time point when 50% of flower buds are open. The calibrated model tries to forecast this specific threshold, but does not infer about any other time point, such as when all buds are open. A bud-population model can fill that gap. 


## Preparation

First the temperature observation needs to be processed into a list of seasons. For the weather handling, I recommend using the [chillR package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/chillR/index.html) [@luedelingChillRStatisticalMethods2024].

```{r weather}
library(evalpheno)

data("cka_weather", package = "evalpheno")
head(cka_weather)

hourly <- chillR::stack_hourly_temps(
  cka_weather, latitude = attr(cka_weather, "latitude")
)$hourtemps
years <- 2008:2009
seasons <- chillR::genSeasonList(hourly, mrange = c(8, 6), years = years)
names(seasons) <- as.character(years)
season <- seasons[[1]]

```

## Sample a bud population and simulate cutting

A population model shares chill and potential heat accumulation among buds,
while selected structure parameters vary. `sd` specifies their standard
deviations; unspecified traits have zero variation. The named parameter vector
supplies the means.

```{r population-sampling}
population_model <- population_pheno_model(
  structure = "phenoflex", n = 100,
  sd = c(yc = 3, zc = 20), seed = 17
)
means <- model_parameters(population_model)
means[c("yc", "zc")] <- c(40, 250)
buds <- sample_population_parameters(population_model, means)
head(buds)
apply(buds, 2, sd)
```

Normal sampling is independent across varying traits. A fixed seed makes the
sample reproducible. `distribution = "normal_skewed"` and, for example,
`skew = c(yc = 2)` enable skew-normal sampling, which requires the optional
`sn` package. Invalid draws raise an error; sampling does not truncate or
resample them. To supply correlated traits, build a valid matrix with the same
columns as `buds` and pass it as `population`.

For this example, interpret the modeled event as budbreak. Sample once and
reuse that population to compare treatments on the same buds:

```{r population-field}
field <- predict_population_phenology(
  population_model, season, parameters = means, population = buds
)
head(field$bloom_jday)
mean(is.finite(field$bloom_jday)) # proportion reaching the event this season
```

Inspect the sampled chill and heat requirements.

```{r plot_samples}
library(ggplot2)

field$population |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  dplyr::select(-s1) |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(tidyselect::everything()) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_grid(~name, scales = 'free') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15)
```

Inspect the predicted flowering dates

```{r plot_bloom}
data.frame(bloom = field$bloom_jday) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = bloom)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  xlab('Day of the year' ) +
  ylab('Predicted share of open flowers (%)') +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15)
```


## Forcing experiment

Temperate fruit trees and their different cultivars vary in their chill and heat requirement. Next to modeling or statistical analysis, the chill requirement is determined by so-called forcing experiments. Branches of the fruit tree are sampled through the winter period and placed under warm conditions. The share of ope flower bud is counted after a fixed amount of days, sometimes it is monitored continuously. It is observed, that the share of budbreak gradually increases through winter with progress of winter. This varying response of different buds on the same branch can be modeled with a bud-population approach. 

For a cutting experiment, identify the hourly row at each cutting date, then
specify a constant forcing temperature and duration.

```{r cutting}
cut_dates <- as.Date(c("2007-11-15", "2007-12-15", "2008-01-15", "2008-02-15", "2008-03-15"))
weather_dates <- as.Date(paste0(season$Year, "-01-01")) + season$JDay - 1
cut_indices <- match(cut_dates, weather_dates)
cutting <- predict_population_phenology(
  population_model, season, parameters = means, population = buds,
  cut_indices = cut_indices, forcing_temperature = 23,
  max_hours_forcing = 21 * 24
)
hours <- cutting$forcing$hours_to_bloom
data.frame(
  cut_date = cut_dates,
  proportion_after_7_days = rowMeans(is.finite(hours) & hours <= 7 * 24),
  proportion_after_21_days = rowMeans(is.finite(hours) & hours <= 21 * 24)
)
```

Elapsed hours are measured from cutting: zero means the bud already reached
the event, and `NA` means it did not within the forcing duration. All buds
remain in the denominator when calculating proportions. Under this model's
forcing assumptions, chill pools stay fixed at cutting, while accumulated
field heat and structure history are retained.

```{r plot_budbreak}
days <- 0:21
proportion <- sapply(days, function(day) {
  rowMeans(is.finite(hours) & hours <= day * 24)
}) |> 
  t() |> 
  as.data.frame()

proportion$days <- 0:21

tidyr::pivot_longer(proportion, cols = -days) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(name = factor(name, levels = paste0('V', 1:length(cut_dates)), 
                       labels = as.character(cut_dates))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = days, y = value, col = name)) +
  geom_line()+
  xlab('Day of the year' ) +
  ylab('Predicted share of open flowers (%)') +
  labs(col="Cutting date") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15) 
```
